parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones a restaurant to book a birthday party.
script: Good afternoon, Bella Vista restaurant, Luca speaking.
Hello. I'd like to book a table for a birthday party, please.
Certainly. What name is it under?
Coles. C, O, L, E, S. Diane Coles.
Thank you. What date were you thinking of?
I originally said twenty, but two people can't come, so eighteen.
Eighteen. Our upstairs room is already booked that evening, but the garden room is free. It has glass doors that open onto the garden.
What time would you like to arrive?
For groups of more than twelve, we ask guests to choose from a set menu. It's thirty-two pounds per person for three courses.
That's fine. Three of the guests are vegetarian.
No problem, there are vegetarian options for every course.
My sister is making a birthday cake. Is it OK to bring it?
Of course. We don't charge for that, and we'll provide candles and plates.
Wonderful. Can we play some music?
You can bring your own music for the garden room, but it has to finish by eleven p.m., because of our neighbours.
Understood. Do you need a deposit?
Yes, a deposit of one hundred pounds, which will be taken off the final bill.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: An organiser gives information about a charity fun run.
script: Hi everyone. I'm Kate, and I'm one of the organisers of this year's charity fun run. Thanks for coming to this information session.

First, where the money goes. In previous years, we've supported the animal shelter and local schools, but this year all the money raised will go to the children's hospital, to buy new equipment for the children's ward.
The run is five kilometres. We did consider a ten-kilometre route, but we want everyone to be able to take part, including families with young children. You can walk the whole way if you like.
If you haven't registered yet, you can do so online until the end of the month. We won't be taking registrations on the day of the race.
Every runner will receive a medal at the finish. And anyone who raises more than a hundred pounds will also get a free T-shirt.
Now, the route. We start at the main gates of Victoria Park. From there, you run along the path by the river. There's a water station about halfway round, next to the lake.
After the water station, the route goes over a bridge, where you'll get a great view of the old town. The first aid tent will be near the bandstand, in the centre of the park.
The finish line is in front of the museum, where there'll be music and food stalls.
If you need to leave a bag, there's a bag drop in the cricket pavilion, near the start.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Noor and James, compare two articles about noise and health.
script: Noor, have you finished reading both articles on urban noise?
Yes. I found the first one interesting, but I think its main weakness is that the sample was so small. Only forty people.
I agree. That's the biggest problem. The second one is much larger. How did they collect their data?
They used recordings from a smartphone app that thousands of volunteers installed. It measured noise levels wherever they went.
That noise didn't just affect sleep. Children in schools near airports actually learned to read more slowly.
Yes, that was striking. So what should our presentation focus on? I don't think we need to explain all the health effects in detail.
No, everyone in the seminar knows the basics. Let's focus on solutions for cities.
Good. And there's one thing I didn't understand in the second article, about how they calculated average exposure.
Why don't we email the author? Researchers are often happy to explain.
Good idea. Now, the solutions. I really like the idea of quieter road surfaces.
Me too. They're expensive, but they reduce traffic noise significantly.
I'd also support noise barriers along motorways.
I'm less keen. They're ugly, and they only protect a few houses. I'd prefer planting more trees. They absorb some noise and have other benefits.
Hmm, I'm not convinced trees make much difference to noise. What about banning night flights?
Definitely. Night-time noise is the most harmful, so I'd support that.
I'd support them in city centres.
I think they just move traffic to other streets, so I'm against them.

options: Airports were the main source of noise.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture on how camels survive in the desert.
script: Today we're looking at one of the best-adapted animals on Earth: the camel.

Let's start with a common misunderstanding. Many people believe that a camel's hump is full of water. In fact, it stores fat, which the camel can use for energy when food is scarce. Storing fat in one place, rather than all over the body, also helps the camel lose heat more easily.

Camels are extraordinary at managing water. They can lose up to thirty percent of their body water and survive, which would kill most mammals. And when they do find water, they can drink up to one hundred litres in about ten minutes.

One reason they can do this is the unusual shape of their red blood cells. Most mammals have round blood cells, but camels' are oval, which allows them to flow even when the blood becomes thick, and to swell without bursting when the camel drinks large amounts quickly.
Camels are also well protected against sandstorms. They have two rows of long eyelashes, and they can close their nostrils to keep out sand.

Another adaptation is their flexible body temperature. A camel's temperature can vary by up to six degrees during the day. Instead of sweating to stay cool, it allows its body to heat up, and loses the heat during the cold desert night. This saves a great deal of water.
Their feet are also adapted, with wide, soft pads that spread out when they walk, so they don't sink into the sand.

Camels were domesticated about three thousand years ago, and they transformed trade across deserts. Today, they're still important in many countries, particularly for their milk, which is rich in vitamin C, an important nutrient in places where fresh fruit is scarce.

passages.title: The Silk Road
paragraphs: The term 'Silk Road' sounds ancient, but it was invented only in 1877, by the German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen. The traders who used the routes never called them by that name. Nor was the Silk Road a single road. It was a vast network of overland routes, together stretching around 6,400 kilometres, which linked China with Central Asia, India, the Middle East and, eventually, the Mediterranean.

The routes began to take shape in the second century BC, when the Chinese Han dynasty sent an official named Zhang Qian westwards. His original mission was diplomatic: he was sent to find allies against the Xiongnu, a nomadic people who threatened China's northern border. Although he failed to form an alliance, and was held captive for years, he returned with detailed reports of wealthy kingdoms to the west. He also reported on the powerful horses of Central Asia, which Chinese emperors were eager to obtain for their armies.

Silk was certainly an important export, highly valued in Rome, where wealthy citizens paid enormous sums for it. But many other goods travelled along the routes, including spices, precious stones, glass, paper and horses. Very few merchants travelled the whole length of the network. Instead, goods passed through the hands of many middlemen, each carrying them a short distance before selling them on, with prices rising at each stage.

The Silk Road carried ideas as well as goods. Buddhism spread from India into Central Asia and China along these routes, and Islam later travelled east in a similar way. The technology of paper-making, developed in China, reached the Islamic world in the eighth century and spread from there to Europe. Musical instruments, artistic styles and foods were exchanged as well.

Not everything that travelled was welcome. Historians believe that the Black Death, the plague that killed a large proportion of Europe's population in the fourteenth century, may have spread westwards along trade routes from Central Asia.

From the fifteenth century, the overland routes gradually declined in importance. Improvements in shipbuilding and navigation meant that sea routes became faster and cheaper for carrying goods between Asia and Europe. Today, however, interest in the Silk Road has returned. In 2014, a section of the network across China, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

passages.title: Science for Everyone
paragraphs: Scientific research is usually imagined as the work of professionals in laboratories. Yet some of the largest scientific projects in the world depend on the help of ordinary people. This is known as citizen science. It is not entirely new: since 1900, thousands of volunteers in North America have taken part in an annual bird count every December, producing one of the longest-running records of wildlife populations anywhere.

The internet has transformed what volunteers can do. In 2007, astronomers at Oxford launched Galaxy Zoo, a website asking members of the public to classify images of galaxies according to their shape. Computers at the time could not do this reliably, and there were far too many images for scientists to examine themselves. More than 100,000 people took part in the first year. One volunteer, a Dutch school teacher named Hanny van Arkel, spotted a strange green cloud that turned out to be a previously unknown type of object.

Citizen science can also take the form of games. Foldit, developed at the University of Washington, challenges players to fold virtual proteins into the most stable shapes. In 2011, players worked out the structure of an enzyme from a virus related to HIV, a problem that had puzzled scientists for around fifteen years. The players solved it in three weeks.

An obvious concern is the quality of data collected by people without scientific training. Researchers have developed several ways to address this. Many projects ask several volunteers to classify the same item and compare their answers, while others provide training and test participants before they begin. Studies have found that, with such safeguards, volunteer data can be as reliable as that produced by professionals.

The benefits go beyond the data itself. Taking part can increase people's understanding of and trust in science. In some cases, citizen science has given communities the tools to investigate problems that affect them directly. Residents near industrial sites, for example, have used low-cost sensors to measure air pollution, providing evidence that they have used to persuade authorities to act.

There are also ethical questions. Volunteers contribute many hours of work, yet they are rarely credited in scientific papers, and some critics argue that their unpaid effort benefits researchers and institutions more than the volunteers themselves. In response, a number of projects now acknowledge volunteers by name, and a few have even listed them as co-authors. Overall, however, the growth of citizen science suggests that, when projects are well designed, the public and professional scientists can achieve things that neither could manage alone.

passages.title: Why Handwriting Still Matters
paragraphs: For centuries, learning to write by hand was one of the central tasks of schooling. Today, many children spend more time typing and tapping on screens than holding a pen, and some education systems have reduced the time spent teaching handwriting. In the United States, for example, national standards introduced in 2010 did not require schools to teach joined-up, or cursive, writing, and many stopped doing so. It is tempting to see handwriting as an outdated skill. I believe that would be a mistake.

Some of the most widely cited evidence concerns note-taking. In a 2014 study, the psychologists Pam Mueller and Daniel Oppenheimer asked students to watch lectures and take notes either on laptops or by hand. Students using laptops wrote more, but they tended to copy the lecture word for word. Those writing by hand, who could not keep up with the speaker, had to summarise ideas in their own words, and they performed better on questions that tested conceptual understanding.

However, the picture is more complicated than headlines suggested. Later attempts to repeat the study produced mixed results, with some finding a smaller advantage for handwriting and others finding none. It would therefore be wrong to claim that students who type their notes always learn less. What seems to matter is not the tool itself but how actively students process information.

The evidence for young children is stronger. Research led by the psychologist Karin James found that children who practised writing letters by hand, rather than typing or tracing them, later showed more activity in brain areas associated with reading when they looked at letters. Writing by hand appears to help children learn to recognise letters, perhaps because each attempt produces a slightly different shape, forcing the brain to identify what all versions have in common.

Studies using brain scans have reached similar conclusions in older students. Researchers in Norway, recording the electrical activity of the brain, found that writing by hand produced more widespread connectivity between brain regions than typing. Such studies cannot show exactly how this affects learning, but they suggest that handwriting engages the brain in distinctive ways.

None of this means that schools should reject technology. Typing is an essential skill, and for many students with physical difficulties, keyboards make writing possible. In my view, the answer is balance: children should be taught both to write fluently by hand and to type efficiently, and handwriting should remain a core part of the curriculum, particularly in the early years of school.

task1.text: The bar chart below shows the percentage of electricity generated from renewable sources in five countries in 2005 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The bar chart compares the proportion of electricity produced from renewable sources in Brazil, Germany, the UK, India and the USA in 2005 and 2025.
Overall, the share of renewable electricity increased in all five countries. Brazil had by far the highest proportion in both years, while Germany and the UK recorded the most dramatic growth.

In 2005, 84% of Brazil's electricity already came from renewable sources, far more than in any other country. India was a distant second at 16%, followed by Germany at 10%, the USA at 9% and the UK at just 4%.

By 2025, Brazil's figure had risen slightly to 89%. The most striking changes, however, were in Germany and the UK, where the proportion rose more than fivefold to 55% and twelvefold to 50% respectively. India and the USA also saw increases, but these were more modest: India's share reached 28%, while the USA's almost tripled to 24%, the lowest of the five countries.

task2.text: In many countries, people are living longer, and the proportion of older people in the population is increasing. What problems does this cause, and what solutions can you suggest? Write at least 250 words.
model: Thanks to better healthcare and living conditions, people in many countries are living longer than ever before. While this is a remarkable achievement, an ageing population creates serious challenges, particularly for public finances and care services. However, these problems can be reduced through sensible policies.

The most significant problem is economic. As the proportion of retired people grows, there are fewer workers paying taxes to support pensions and public services. In countries such as Japan and Italy, governments are already struggling to fund pensions without raising taxes or borrowing heavily. A second problem is pressure on healthcare and social care. Older people are more likely to suffer from long-term conditions such as heart disease and dementia, which require expensive treatment and care. Many families also find it difficult to look after elderly relatives while working full-time.

There are several ways to address these issues. Firstly, governments can gradually raise the retirement age to reflect longer life expectancy, since many people now remain healthy and able to work into their late sixties. Encouraging flexible and part-time work for older employees would also allow them to continue contributing to the economy. Secondly, investment in preventive healthcare, such as programmes that encourage exercise and healthy diets, can reduce the number of people who develop serious illnesses. Finally, technology may help, for example through devices that allow elderly people to live safely and independently in their own homes for longer.

In conclusion, an ageing population puts pressure on public finances and care systems, but by extending working lives, focusing on prevention and using technology, societies can benefit from longer lives rather than being burdened by them.

speaking.cue:
Describe a book you enjoyed reading.
You should say:
- what the book was
- when you read it
- what it was about
and explain why you enjoyed it.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about a book called Sapiens by Yuval Noah Harari, which I read during my second year at university. A friend lent it to me because she knew I was interested in how technology changes society. The book tells the history of humans, from the first species of humans living in Africa to the present day. What I found fascinating was the way the author connects big ideas. For example, he argues that what made humans so successful wasn't just intelligence, but our ability to believe in shared stories, like money, nations and companies, which allow millions of strangers to cooperate. I'd never thought about money as a kind of story before, and it completely changed the way I look at the world. I also enjoyed it because it's written in a very clear and sometimes funny style, so even though it covers complicated topics, it never felt like a textbook. I didn't agree with everything he says, especially some of his predictions about the future, but that's partly why I liked it. It made me think and argue with my friends about it for weeks.
